metaDescription: Six 16 to 18 inch corded electric tillers under $200 compared on amps, six-tine heads, overload protection, depth and storage for garden beds.
expertTake: The Westinghouse 18-inch 15 amp is the best overall for the most motor and a stated 9-inch depth. The LawnMaster TE1318M is the value pick for its overload protection. Anyone clearing fresh sod or heavy clay should skip all of these and rent a gas rear-tine tiller.
introParagraphs: Two hundred dollars is where corded electric tillers stop being toys. The machines here have real motors, wide heads and six-tine rotors that can turn a vegetable plot in an afternoon, provided the soil is already workable.

The cap here is $200, and prices move, so it reflects listing prices when this guide was updated. At this level the differences are motor reserve, how the machine protects itself from stalls, and how well it folds for storage.

products.name: Westinghouse 18-Inch 15 Amp Corded Electric Tiller
products.description:
The Westinghouse pairs a 15-amp motor with an 18-inch head carrying six sets of four integrated steel blades on an 8-inch diameter rotor. A 15-amp motor is about 1,800 watts, the most a standard household circuit can deliver, and tine speed reaches about 400 RPM, slightly faster than the 360 to 380 RPM of rivals.

The integrated blade design means the tines are part of a single assembly rather than loose bolt-on pieces, which resists bending on buried stones and avoids loose hardware. It lists a stated depth of up to 9 inches, which in practice means 5 to 6 inches on a first pass in firm soil, deeper on a second.

Compared with the 13.5-amp LawnMaster it has one and a half more amps of reserve, which shows in compacted soil. The trade is that it does not advertise a stall-protection clutch, so a stuck tine can burn the motor if you lean on it. Use a 14 AWG cord under 50 feet and keep it behind you. Rinse and dry the blades after each session. At year three, the usual wear points are the cord strain relief and the tine bolts, both easy to inspect before each season.
products.bestFor: Larger beds and firmer soil where the most corded motor matters.
pros: 15 amp motor has the most reserve in the group
Integrated six-set blade head resists bending
cons: Draws the full capacity of a 15 amp circuit

products.name: LawnMaster TE1318M 13.5 Amp 18-Inch Electric Tiller
products.description:
LawnMaster builds this around six rust-resistant steel blades at 380 RPM and an 18-inch path, with mechanical overload protection that shuts the tines off if they hit a stone or root. That clutch is the feature that sets it apart: it protects the gearbox and motor from the sudden shock load of a locked tine, a common cause of tiller failure.

The 13.5-amp motor is about 1,600 watts, a notch below the 15-amp Westinghouse, but the overload protection makes up for that in reliability if your soil is full of stones. It is aimed at medium to large gardens, per the listing, with a 9-inch stated depth.

Expect two passes for full depth, and clear large rocks first. LawnMaster is an established mid-tier brand, so spare tines and manuals are readily available. Unplug before clearing tangles and store it with the handle folded. The same clutch also forgives a beginner who leans on the handle, which makes it a sensible first purchase for someone new to tilling.
products.bestFor: Stony or root-filled garden soil where gearbox protection matters.
pros: Mechanical overload cutoff protects the gearbox
18 inch path with a 9 inch stated depth
cons: 13.5 amps has less reserve than 15 amps
Stalls briefly rather than pushing through

products.name: BILT HARD 18-Inch 15 Amp Corded Electric Tiller
products.description:
The BILT HARD gives you a 15-amp motor, an 18-inch head and six steel tines spinning at 380 RPM, in a body that weighs only 25 pounds. Four quick bolt knobs fold the handles flat for storage, which is a real benefit when the machine lives on a garage shelf.

Against the Westinghouse it matches the amperage and gives up about 20 RPM and the integrated-blade design. Against the LawnMaster it has more power but no stated overload clutch. Light weight is a double-edged feature: it carries easily, but a 25-pound machine has less mass to resist bouncing, so let the tines do the work.

The handle-fold design is convenient but check the knobs for tightness before each session, since vibration can loosen them. Keep the cord short and heavy and clean the tines after use. A good choice for an owner who values storage and portability. A fold-flat machine also tends to survive a garage better, because it spends the winter on a shelf and not on a damp floor.
products.bestFor: Owners who must lift and store the machine regularly.
pros: Handles fold with four quick knobs
Easy to carry to remote beds
cons: Light body can bounce in firm soil

products.name: BILT HARD 16-Inch 13.5 Amp Foldable Electric Tiller
products.description:
This BILT HARD sits in the middle of its range: a 13.5-amp AC motor, a 16-inch path and six steel blades at 360 RPM. The listing quotes a motor speed near 19,000 RPM, but as with all tillers that is the motor, not the tines, which spin at 360 RPM after the gear reduction.

Compared with the 18-inch BILT HARD it trades two inches of width for a lower price and an easier fit between rows. Compared with the Sun Joe TJ603E it adds 1.5 amps of motor. Foldable handles keep it compact on a shelf.

It suits small to mid-size gardens. Take shallow first passes, keep the cord short and check the fasteners on the handle each season. If you later need more width, the 18-inch version of this machine shares the same layout, so nothing about the controls has to be relearned.
products.bestFor: Mid-size gardens that want more motor than a 12 amp unit.
pros: 13.5 amp motor in a 16 inch body
cons: Listing motor RPM can mislead buyers

products.name: Sun Joe TJ603E 16-Inch 12 Amp Corded Electric Tiller
products.description:
The Sun Joe TJ603E is the long-running budget workhorse: a 12-amp motor, a 16-inch path and six angled steel tines on a rotary head, with a folding handle for storage. It lacks the headline amps of the 15-amp machines but has a track record of availability and parts.

At 12 amps it draws around 1,400 watts, so it is a notch below the 13.5-amp BILT HARD 16-inch. It is a good fit for loose soil and annual bed prep rather than compacted clay. Sun Joe has wide dealer and spare-part support, which makes the second and third year of ownership easier.

Use a 14 AWG extension cord, make two shallow passes, and store it dry. Because the brand has been selling similar tillers for years, replacement tines are commonly stocked, which is the best insurance against a bent blade.
products.bestFor: Annual bed prep in loose soil where parts support matters.
pros: 12 amp draw is easy on circuits
cons: 12 amps stalls sooner in compacted soil

products.name: LawnMaster TE1216M 12 Amp 16-Inch Electric Tiller
products.description:
The LawnMaster TE1216M is the 12-amp, 16-inch sibling of the 18-inch TE1318M, with a stated 9-inch cutting depth, rust-resistant blades and a mechanical clutch. The clutch protects the drivetrain from jams, which gives it a reliability angle that other 12-amp units lack.

Against the Sun Joe TJ603E it matches the amps and the width but adds the clutch and a stated depth. Against the larger TE1318M it gives up two inches of width and 1.5 amps, which makes it cheaper and lighter.

It works best for loosened beds and compost mixing. Unplug before clearing tines and keep the machine dry between uses. For a gardener who tills once in spring and again in autumn, that clutch can be the difference between a ten-year machine and a three-year one.
products.bestFor: Smaller gardens that want drivetrain protection at a modest size.
cons: 16 inch path takes more passes than 18 inch rivals

buyingCriteria.explanation: The 15-amp Westinghouse and BILT HARD 18-inch deliver about 1,800 watts, while the 12-amp Sun Joe and LawnMaster TE1216M deliver about 1,400. That 400-watt gap is the difference between plowing through and bogging in compacted soil. Do not confuse amps with tine speed, which stays near 360 to 400 RPM on every model here. Owners who buy the cheapest 12-amp unit for heavy soil are the most common source of disappointed reviews.

A tine that hits a buried stone stops instantly, sending shock into the gearbox. The LawnMaster pair lists a mechanical clutch or overload cutoff, which slips or disengages instead. Without one, take shallow passes and clear rocks first. A clutch is also a useful hint about how the maker thinks about durability overall.

An 18-inch machine covers 12 percent more ground per pass than a 16-inch one, but it is bulkier. Foldable handles, as on both BILT HARD models and the Sun Joe, cut storage space by half. Measure your shed shelf before buying. Also check the weight if you must lift the tiller into a truck bed or over a step.

Integrated blade assemblies, like the Westinghouse's 6 x 4 design, resist bending better than loose bolt-on tines. Six tines break soil finer than four. Rust-resistant coatings help, but dry storage matters more. Thin tines that bend on the first buried rock are the single most common repair.

A 15-amp load on a thin or long cord causes voltage drop, which heats the motor. Use 14 AWG up to 50 feet and 12 AWG beyond. Never use a coiled cord under load. A cord reel with a heavy lead is a better investment than a longer cheap cord.
All six models quote 8 to 9 inches. In firm soil you will get 5 to 6 inches on a first pass. Plan on two passes at different angles. Wet clay will defeat all six machines, so wait a day after rain.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor reserve
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared amps across the group. The two 15-amp machines scored highest, the 13.5-amp pair next and the 12-amp pair lowest. Extra credit went to machines that state a rating the circuit can support.

howWeEvaluated.title: Drivetrain protection
howWeEvaluated.description: We credited overload cutoffs and clutches, listed on the LawnMaster TE1318M and TE1216M.

howWeEvaluated.title: Tine assembly
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored the Westinghouse's integrated 6 x 4 blades over loose tines. We cross-checked the claimed blade assembly against the images in each listing.

howWeEvaluated.title: Storage and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed weight and folding handles. The 25-pound BILT HARD 18 inch led on portability.

howWeEvaluated.title: Owner feedback patterns
howWeEvaluated.description: We evaluated owner patterns on bent tines, loosened knobs and cord damage.

cards.label: 15 amp
cards.text: The Westinghouse and BILT HARD 18-inch use the full circuit and drive harder in firm soil. They need a heavy cord and a free circuit.

cards.label: 12 to 13.5 amp
cards.text: The Sun Joe, LawnMaster pair and BILT HARD 16-inch are easier on circuits and fine for worked soil.

howToChoose.note: Pick 15 amps for firm soil, 12 to 13.5 for beds you till every year.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: An overload clutch or cutoff, and shallow passes. Remove large stones first.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The LawnMaster TE1318M at 13.5 amps with its mechanical cutoff is the safest choice for stones.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Your beds are firm or over 200 square feet, which points to the Westinghouse over the Sun Joe.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your soil is loose and annual prep is all you need, where the Sun Joe or TE1216M is plenty.

maintenance.why: Wet soil rusts the steel. A dry rinse takes a minute.
Seeping grease signals a worn seal.

faq.a: For firm soil, yes. For loose, previously worked beds, 12 to 13.5 amps are enough. Higher amps also demand a better cord. Smaller amps also work, but with more passes and more patience.
It slips when the tines jam, protecting the gearbox. It does not make the tiller stronger, only more durable. It will not make the machine stronger, only longer lived.
Not well. Cut and lift sod first, or use a gas tiller. A sod cutter or a rented machine makes the first pass; the electric tiller maintains the bed.
Expect 5 to 6 inches on the first pass, up to the stated 8 or 9 inches with repeat passes. A stiff, dry bed may need a day of watering first.

faq.q: What does $200 buy over cheaper tillers?
faq.a: More amps, wider heads and stall protection. Prices move and the cap reflects listing prices when this guide was updated. Compare the listed price against the cap on the day you buy.
Quieter than gas, but you still need hearing protection for long sessions. Foam earmuffs and eye protection are cheap and worth using.
